newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: RUGBY UNION-SMITH SET TO CLAIM TEST LOOSE-HEAD BERTH.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-SMITH SET TO CLAIM TEST LOOSE-HEAD BERTH.

text.p: Scotland's loose-head prop Tom Smith, whose scrummaging and all-round mobility have impressed the tour management, has a golden opportunity to claim a British Lions test place when he packs down against the Natal Sharks at Kings Park on Saturday.

"Tom's scrummaging went very well against the Gauteng Lions on Wednesday night. He's a very dynamic player and, the more dynamic players we have in the side, the better," Lions coach Ian McGeechan said.
"We'd like to see him again in a slightly different pack and that is why we've changed the make-up of the front five for the match against Natal."
While the Lions three-quarters have thrilled South African crowds with their slick handling, pace and creativity, the overall form of the tight forwards has been erratic.

The Lions' strong men were embarrassed time and again by the powerful Western Province front row in the third match of their tour and initial plans by the selectors to focus on the core of the England pack for the test matches appear to be changing.

Significantly, there are only four England players in the side to take on defending Currie Cup champions Natal this Saturday and that number would have been three had English lock Simon Shaw not replaced injured Irishman Jeremy Davidson who has a hamstring strain.

Although still two games away from deciding their test match combination, the Lions selectors could well settle for non-English forwards in Irish hooker Keith Wood, prop Smith, Irish lock Davidson and Irish number eight Eric Miller, if he performs well in that position against Natal.

Former English flyhalf Stuart Barnes detects a feeling in the Lions camp that the English forwards - although bigger and generally stronger than their Scottish, Irish and Welsh counterparts - have taken longer to adapt to the more mobile game now requred by modern rugby.

"Probably because the other Home Nations don't have the player resources which England enjoys, their forwards often seem to be a lot quicker in taking on board different approaches and playing styles. That seems to be the case on this Lions tour," Bares said.
Despite the initial problems, Lions forwards coach Jim Telfer believes the team's scrummaging is improving.

"I think the scrummaging against the Gauteng Lions on Wednesday was very good. We've changed our technique, worked very hard on it and we've looked at different combinations all the time," Telfer said.

"The competition from other players also has a very beneficial effect - and the players respond well to pressure. They're now looking over their shoulders and they must realise they are not playing for themselves but for the team. Our players must beable to lay their bodies on the line."
